entry.title: We Should Not Need a Courtroom: Part Four
entry.summary:
The country had a version of this conversation in 2002, during the Andrea Yates trial. More than twenty years later, the research has not moved nearly as far as the outrage has.

More
entry.content:
This is Part Four of a four-part essay. Start with Part One.

Part Four: We Still Do Not Know Enough

The country had a version of this conversation in 2002, during the Andrea Yates trial. A Texas jury convicted her. An appeals court later overturned the conviction, and in 2006 a second jury, hearing the same case, found her not guilty by reason of insanity. More than twenty years later, the research has not moved nearly as far as the outrage has.

Postpartum psychosis still does not have its own diagnosis in the DSM. The closest the manual comes is a specifier, with peripartum onset, attached to another mood or psychotic disorder, and the experts who study this illness say even that describes its timing inaccurately.

In October 2025, an international group of those experts published a consensus statement in Biological Psychiatry arguing that postpartum psychosis should be classified as a distinct condition within the bipolar disorders, with its own timing and criteria. Their reasons were concrete. Most women who have it show prominent mood symptoms. It responds very well to lithium and to electroconvulsive therapy, the same treatments used for severe bipolar illness. About half of women with a first episode go on to develop bipolar disorder. The panel's argument was practical: an illness without its own classification is easier to miss and slower to treat, and that delay has cost lives.

What is striking is how much is already known, and how little of it reaches the women who need it.

We know the window. The risk is concentrated in the first weeks after birth to a degree few illnesses in psychiatry can match. We know who is at highest risk: women with bipolar disorder, and women who have already had an episode. A woman who has had postpartum psychosis once faces roughly a one in three chance of it returning after a later birth.

We also know that in many cases it can be prevented. In a Dutch study published in 2012, women with a history of postpartum psychosis alone who started lithium immediately after delivery did not relapse. Among those who declined it, more than four in ten did. The study was small and needs to be repeated. What it shows is that the risk can be identified during pregnancy, before the baby arrives, if someone asks the right questions.

Asking the right questions is where the system breaks down.

Most postpartum screening is built for depression. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that pediatricians screen mothers for postpartum depression at the one, two, four, and six month well-baby visits, which makes sense, since a new mother sees her baby's doctor far more often than her own. Those screening tools are designed to find depression. They are not designed to catch the early signs of mania or psychosis, and psychosis usually arrives before the first of those visits.

When a woman does need a hospital, the options in this country are thin. Postpartum Support International's directory lists five inpatient perinatal psychiatric units in the United States. None of them admits the baby to stay overnight with the mother. England, France, and Australia have had mother and baby units for decades, where mother and infant are admitted together. Most American women who need inpatient psychiatric care after a birth are admitted to a general psychiatric unit, away from an infant they may still be trying to nurse.

More research is needed, and it is needed for reasons that go beyond any single case. While the public was focused on the rarest outcome there is, the more common danger got almost no attention. In data from maternal mortality review committees in thirty-six states, compiled by the CDC for 2017 through 2019, mental health conditions, including suicide and overdose, were the leading underlying cause of pregnancy-related death, at nearly a quarter. The committees judged more than four in five pregnancy-related deaths overall to be preventable. In an earlier CDC analysis, nearly two thirds of the mental health deaths happened between six weeks and a year after delivery, long after most women have had their last postpartum appointment.

That is where women are actually dying, and it is largely preventable.

Fear-based messaging makes this worse. If the only thing a new mother hears about postpartum illness is danger, she is less likely to tell anyone when something feels wrong, because she is afraid of what will happen if she does. What helps is women and families knowing the signs, and knowing that these conditions respond to treatment.

The most useful thing anyone can do with all of this is ask the new mothers in your life how they are really doing, and ask the people around them what has changed, because family often sees what a short appointment cannot. And if what you hear worries you, help her get to someone who specializes in this.

I say that as a woman who went through postpartum depression three times, and as a psychologist who would send her to that specialist rather than treat her myself.

For free, confidential support during or after pregnancy, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-852-6262. Call or text 988 during a mental health crisis. If someone is in immediate danger or appears to be experiencing postpartum psychosis, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

entry.title: We Should Not Need a Courtroom: Part Three
entry.summary:
I heard someone use the phrase stay-at-home jurors, and I have not stopped thinking about it.

More
entry.content:
This is Part Three of a four-part essay. Start with Part One.

Part Three: The Stay-at-Home Jurors

I heard someone use the phrase stay-at-home jurors, and I have not stopped thinking about it.

The trial was livestreamed, and people watched it the way they watch everything now: in pieces, on their phones, between other things. They watched a witness, saw a clip, read someone else's interpretation, and formed an opinion.

What reached most people was a selection. Someone chose the forty seconds worth posting, someone else wrote the caption, and the comment section supplied the rest. A witness breaking down on the stand travels. Three hours of testimony about medical records does not.

Social media has given people the sense that watching part of a trial qualifies them to decide the whole case. The opinions that determined the verdict belonged to the jurors who were actually there.

Think about what a juror does. Jurors sit through weeks of testimony. They hear the evidence the court has determined they may consider, and they are told not to read coverage of the case or discuss it with anyone while it is going on. They receive instructions about the law and the burden of proof, and they are required to follow those instructions even when the law does not match their instincts.

Then they deliberate with other people who also heard the whole case. They have to explain their thinking, listen to disagreement, and remain open to changing their minds.

Afterward, they go home and live with the decision.

People watching from home carry none of that responsibility. They can skip testimony, turn it off, return later, or rely on clips selected by someone else. They do not have to apply the legal standard. They do not have to deliberate with anyone. Their conclusions have no effect on the verdict.

Still, they often become certain very quickly.

Certainty feels the same from the inside whether or not we have enough information to support it. Nothing warns us that our opinion is underinformed. The person who sat through every day of testimony and the person who watched a few minutes before bed can feel equally sure.

Watching also carries its own kind of confidence, the sense of having seen it with your own eyes. A viewer who watches a woman sit quietly at a defense table may feel she has learned something about that woman's mind. What she has learned is how the woman looked in a courtroom, long after the day in question. In the second part of this essay I wrote about periods of lucidity, and how often they are taken as proof that nothing was wrong. A calm face on a livestream invites the same mistake.

That brings me to the difference between compassion and judgment, which is the part I most want readers to sit with.

When an older person comes out of surgery confused, agitated, or paranoid, perhaps accusing a family member of something terrible, we may recognize delirium. We understand that something has happened to the person's brain. When the delirium clears, we are usually able to place the behavior inside the illness. Nobody concludes that the grandfather who accused his daughter of stealing from him in the recovery room had secretly believed it all along.

We can understand that with delirium, a high fever, dangerously low blood sugar, or a stroke that temporarily changes someone's personality and behavior.

We become less generous when the person is a mother.

Motherhood gets treated as an identity, so anything a mother does, under almost any condition, becomes evidence of who she really was. That is why so many people kept asking how a mother could stop loving her children.

I think that is the wrong question to ask about a psychiatric emergency.

In the first part of this essay I described how quickly I read my own depression as a verdict on my mothering. I did that privately, to myself. This summer the public did it to a stranger, out loud, by the hundreds of thousands.

I know that none of these medical examples carries the weight of what happened in this case. I am interested in how we assign meaning to behavior. In some conditions, we recognize that the brain has been altered. In others, we decide the behavior reveals the person's character.

So I keep asking myself the same question.

If you entered a state in which your perception, judgment, and behavior were profoundly unlike you, how would you want other people to understand that period? Would you want the worst moment of your life replayed by strangers as proof of who you had always been?

The legal system has a specific job. It determines what happened and then applies the law of that jurisdiction to questions of intent, capacity, and criminal responsibility. Having a psychiatric diagnosis does not answer those questions. The law considers what a severe mental illness did to the person's ability to understand the nature or wrongfulness of the conduct at the time.

Even that depends on where the case is tried. In some states the question is whether a mental illness left the person unable to know what she was doing or that it was wrong. Other states also ask whether she lacked the capacity to conform her conduct to the law. A few states have abolished the insanity defense altogether. Both sides usually bring their own experts, and the experts often disagree. Jurors are asked to sort through all of it and answer the one question their state's law puts to them.

Those are narrow and difficult questions. The public discussion often skipped them.

People moved quickly from believing that she committed the acts to believing they understood her intent, her capacity, her relationship with her children, and the person she had been before that day.

They had pieces of the story. They felt certain anyway.

That is what I keep thinking about when I hear the phrase stay-at-home jurors.

For free, confidential support during or after pregnancy, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-852-6262. Call or text 988 during a mental health crisis. If someone is in immediate danger or appears to be experiencing postpartum psychosis, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

entry.title: We Should Not Need a Courtroom: Part Two
entry.summary:
The difference between postpartum depression, anxiety, OCD, and psychosis is the first thing the culture should have known before this summer, and most people did not.

More
entry.content:
This is Part Two of a four-part essay. Start with Part One.

Part Two: What We Should Have Known First

The difference between postpartum depression, anxiety, OCD, and psychosis is the first thing the culture should have known before this summer, and most people did not.

Those terms get used as if they were one condition at four volumes, a little sad at one end and dangerous at the other. They are separate illnesses. They arrive at different times, carry different risks, and are treated differently. Collapsing them into one word is how a woman with frightening thoughts she would never act on ends up afraid to say them out loud, and how a woman in a psychiatric emergency ends up being told she just needs sleep.

The baby blues are common. They can include crying, irritability, worry, and feeling overwhelmed. They are usually mild and resolve within about two weeks.

Postpartum depression is a clinical depression, and it can be serious. It can begin during pregnancy, and it can begin months after delivery, well after the six-week checkup many women still think of as the end of postpartum care. It can interfere with sleep, concentration, functioning, caregiving, and the ability to feel connected to the baby. It does not always look like visible sadness. Sometimes it looks like anger, numbness, shame, or continuing to do everything that needs to be done while feeling almost nothing.

That last version is the one I know.

Postpartum anxiety can happen with depression or on its own. A mother may feel unable to stop anticipating danger. She may repeatedly check whether the baby is breathing, or lie awake listening even when someone else is caring for the baby.

Postpartum OCD can bring violent, unwanted thoughts or images involving the baby. The mother is usually horrified by them and may hide them because she is afraid of what they mean about her. She may begin checking, avoiding, asking for reassurance, or creating rituals intended to keep the baby safe.

Intrusive thoughts can also occur without OCD. Many new parents have a passing image of dropping the baby on the stairs or of something terrible happening in the bath. The concern grows when the thoughts become persistent, distressing, disruptive, or connected to compulsive behavior.

The distinction between OCD and psychosis is important. In OCD, the thought feels foreign to the mother. She does not want it, and she is frightened by it. In psychosis, a person may experience a delusion as true and have little awareness that she is ill.

A mother with postpartum OCD may avoid bathing her baby because she is terrified by an image of drowning the baby. She is trying to prevent the feared event. A mother experiencing psychosis may believe something about the baby that is untrue but feels completely real to her.

From the outside, both situations may involve disturbing thoughts about a baby. Internally, they are very different experiences, and they call for very different responses. One needs a clinician who understands perinatal OCD and will not panic at what she hears. The other needs an emergency room.

Postpartum psychosis is rare, occurring after roughly one or two of every thousand births. It usually begins quickly, most often within the first days or two weeks after delivery. It is a psychiatric emergency. The risk of a first episode of psychosis with prominent mood symptoms is about twenty-three times higher in the four weeks after birth than at any other point in a woman's life.

Hallucinations and delusions are what most people picture. They are often not what a family sees first. Most women with postpartum psychosis have prominent mood symptoms: mania, a mixed state of mania and depression at once, or a depression severe enough to include psychotic features. The earliest signs can include irritability, confusion, rapidly changing moods, unusual energy, faster speech, agitation, or sleeping very little without appearing tired.

The symptoms can also change quickly. A woman may seem markedly unwell and then have a period in which she appears lucid. Family members and clinicians may interpret those periods as evidence that she is fine or that the earlier behavior was intentional. Periods of lucidity can be part of how the illness presents.

Postpartum psychosis is closely associated with bipolar-spectrum illness. A history of bipolar disorder or a previous episode of postpartum psychosis increases the risk considerably. At the same time, many women who experience it have no previously recognized psychiatric history. Follow-up studies suggest that about half of women who have a first episode later develop bipolar disorder. For some, the postpartum episode is the first visible presentation of an illness they will live with for the rest of their lives.

That means the woman may not know what is happening. Her family may not know. They may be trying to distinguish ordinary exhaustion from mania, anxiety from obsessive fear, and sleep deprivation from the beginning of a psychiatric emergency, at three in the morning, with a newborn in the next room.

Most families have never been taught how to make those distinctions.

Women are told about gestational diabetes. They are warned about preeclampsia and hemorrhage. The information about mental illness exists. The Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health's list of urgent maternal warning signs puts thoughts of harming yourself or your baby on the same list as chest pain, heavy bleeding, and trouble breathing. Whether a woman ever sees that list, and whether anyone sits down and explains it to her partner or her mother before discharge, is another matter. Many leave the hospital without clear information about postpartum mental illness, what symptoms require immediate attention, or where to go for help.

A great many people learned about postpartum psychosis for the first time from a courtroom.

If you have experienced violent or frightening intrusive thoughts and have been afraid to disclose them, the thoughts alone do not mean that you want to act on them. Tell a clinician who understands perinatal OCD. It is common and treatable.

If someone becomes confused, delusional, paranoid, unusually energized despite little sleep, or disconnected from reality after giving birth, seek emergency psychiatric care.

For free, confidential support during or after pregnancy, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-852-6262. Call or text 988 during a mental health crisis. If someone is in immediate danger or appears to be experiencing postpartum psychosis, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

entry.title: We Should Not Need a Courtroom: Part One
entry.summary:
I had postpartum depression three times.

The first time, I did not really know what it was. I had just had a baby and everything had changed, and I assumed the disconnection and the flat mood were part of that.

More
entry.content:
Part One: Three Times

I had postpartum depression three times.

The first time, I did not know that was what it was. I had just had a baby, and every part of my life had changed. Before her, I had been hyper independent. I worked. I loved my work. I could decide what to do with my time and where to go. Then there was a newborn who needed me to feed her, hold her, and keep her alive. I was no longer independent of another person’s needs, even for a few hours.

I assumed the disconnection and flatness were part of adjusting to motherhood. I saw other women who were pregnant or holding their babies, and they seemed happy in a way I was not. I thought something was wrong with me. I connected it to my trauma history and treated my inability to feel what I believed a mother should feel as evidence of some defect in me.

I did not understand that depression could interfere with the feeling of connection itself. I loved my baby, but I could not always feel the emotional attachment I believed was supposed to arrive with her.

The second time, I knew it was postpartum depression.

My daughters were nineteen months apart. There were now two babies, and for several months, I felt resentful that the second one had made my life harder. She had not done anything wrong, of course. She was a quiet, easy baby who was deeply attached to me. But depression has a way of attaching the burden to the person who needs you most.

Because I recognized it the second time, I gave myself space to adjust. I believed my body was recovering from the hormones, physical trauma, and exhaustion of giving birth. In my mind, if it took nine months to have a baby, it could reasonably take nine months to recover from having one. I did not expect myself to return immediately to who I had been before.

I remember when something changed.

She was about five months old. Someone reached to take her from me, and she grabbed my shirt and buried her face in my shoulder. In that moment, I felt an overwhelming rush of love for her. It was not that I had begun loving her at five months old. The love had been there. I simply had not been able to feel it in that way. It had seemed chemically blocked, and then, suddenly, it was available to me.

The third time was worse.

It lasted somewhere between seven and nine months. I felt flat, overwhelmed, and sad. I also felt ashamed that something appeared to be wrong with me because I had not experienced the immediate emotional attachment to my babies that mothers are expected to describe.

I loved them. I cared for them. I kept going. But love as a commitment and love as an accessible feeling were not always the same experience.

When people suggested medication, I initially felt resentful. I heard the recommendation as confirmation that I was failing at motherhood. My memory is that I eventually did take medication because the depression lasted so long. What remains clearest is not the medication itself. It is how difficult it was to separate needing help from the belief that needing help meant I was not doing my job as a mother.

My experiences do not establish what another woman should do. They are not an argument for waiting, refusing medication, or assuming that postpartum symptoms will resolve on their own. They are simply what happened to me.

They also shaped my compassion for women who experience perinatal mental illness. Some women experience postpartum depression once and never again. Some have a different experience after each birth. Mine became progressively worse.

I am a psychologist, but I do not specialize in treating perinatal mood and anxiety disorders. If a woman came to my office a few weeks after giving birth in significant distress, I would refer her to someone with specific training in this area. Having lived through postpartum depression does not make me qualified to treat it. Personal experience and clinical expertise are not interchangeable.

My experience with depression also tells me very little about postpartum anxiety, postpartum OCD, or postpartum psychosis. Postpartum psychosis is not simply a more severe version of postpartum depression. It is a different illness that requires specialized assessment and treatment.

What my experience does help me understand is how quickly a woman can interpret her suffering as a moral failure.

We have created a remarkably narrow story about motherhood. A woman is expected to want a baby, enjoy being pregnant, feel transformed by childbirth, and experience immediate, uncomplicated love when the baby is placed in her arms.

That was not my experience.

I had not wanted to become a mother. When I became pregnant, I decided to become one, but I was not excited. I was terrified. I eventually became a very good mother, which was not something I initially believed I would be able to do. But becoming a good mother did not make pregnancy, childbirth, or caring for babies beautiful or easy.

My pregnancies were physically difficult. I gained a great deal of weight. My babies were large, between eight and nine pounds, and I went beyond my due date with two of them. Childbirth was physically and emotionally stressful. Motherhood changed my relationship with my body, my work, my independence, my finances, and my understanding of myself.

The first two times, I did not have a supportive husband or father beside me in the way I needed. He simply was not there. The father of my third child was supportive of her, but I do not know that he was particularly supportive of me. Supporting a baby is not always the same as supporting the woman who gave birth to one.

You can want to be a mother and hate having babies. You can love your children and grieve the life you had before them. You can care for a baby responsibly while feeling detached, resentful, frightened, or overwhelmed. None of those experiences fit comfortably inside the version of motherhood we prefer to discuss.

This summer, a trial involving a mother and postpartum psychosis became something much of the country watched and debated. I will not offer a clinical opinion about the woman at the center of it. I never evaluated her, and offering a diagnosis or forensic conclusion about someone you have never met violates an important boundary in my profession.

What disturbed me was the certainty with which so many other people did exactly that.

People formed conclusions about her illness, her intentions, her motherhood, and her character from pieces of a story. They spoke as though a woman’s behavior at the most catastrophic point of an illness explained everything about who she had been before it.

I do not know her full story. Most of the people commenting on it do not know it either. That should have made us more careful. Instead, it often made us more certain.

My three experiences with postpartum depression do not give me the authority to explain postpartum psychosis. They do, however, leave me with a lasting memory of how easily suffering can become evidence against a mother. We ask whether she loved her children before we ask what happened to her. We judge her response before we understand the illness. We expect motherhood to override biology, trauma, sleep deprivation, isolation, physical recovery, and the loss of a former life.

When it does not, we decide something is wrong with the woman.

Sometimes something is wrong. But illness is not the same as moral failure, and understanding that distinction should be where the conversation begins.

If you or someone you know is struggling after a birth, call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-852-6262. Call or text 988 during a mental health crisis.

entry.title: The Distance Between Us: Part Four
entry.summary:
Part Four: What Repair Can and Cannot Do

Repair is one of the most misunderstood words in estrangement. People hear it and picture reunion. Sometimes that happens. Repair does not always mean closeness, though.

More
entry.content:
Part Four: What Repair Can and Cannot Do

Repair is one of the most misunderstood words in estrangement. People hear it and picture reunion: the phone call, the apology, the holiday table, the grandchild placed back in someone's arms, the sibling text thread revived. Sometimes that happens, and people find their way back to each other in a form that is humbler and more honest than what they had before. Repair does not always mean closeness, though.

Sometimes it means the person who left no longer needs hatred to hold the boundary, or the person who was left stops using their pain as proof of innocence. It can be a letter that is never answered but is finally free of accusation. It can be telling the truth privately without requiring anyone to validate it. It can be no contact that continues while the nervous system stops organizing itself around the wound. That still counts.

The fantasy version goes like this. Everyone finally understands everything. The person who left grasps how painful the silence has been, the person who was left grasps how much damage came before it, and both turn toward each other with perfect language and perfect remorse. Nobody gets defensive or minimizes or reaches for the oldest weapon in the room. That is rarely how it begins.

Repair usually starts much smaller, when one person can tell the truth without turning it into a courtroom, or can say I can see that my version is not the only version here. It starts when an apology becomes specific enough to matter. I'm sorry for whatever you think I did is not that apology. Neither is I'm sorry you feel that way, or I guess I was just a terrible parent, or after all this time, can't we just move on? Those are escape routes.

A repair attempt carries weight when it names the injury without demanding absolution on the spot:

I can see that when I dismissed your anxiety, you learned not to bring your feelings to me.

I can see that when I made you responsible for my emotions, you had to become careful around me.

I can see that when I denied what happened, the denial may have hurt you again.

I can see that my intention to protect you did not change the fact that you felt controlled.

I can see that I wanted closeness, but I often reached for it through guilt.

Specificity is what separates remorse from performance.

For the person who left, repair may ask for a different kind of work. Distance can be necessary. Sometimes it is the first honest decision a person has ever made. Distance can also harden into an identity. The protector part that once saved you can keep scanning for danger long after the immediate danger has passed, reading every imperfect word as proof that nothing has changed and mistaking softness for surrender. That does not make the boundary wrong. It means the boundary may need to be held consciously rather than by reflex.

I am not in contact because contact harms me is a different internal statement from I am not in contact because the protector in me cannot imagine any other way to keep the younger part safe. The conclusion may be identical, and no contact may remain the right answer. The first is a boundary. The second is exile, guarded by fear.

The goal is not to force reconciliation. The goal is choice, on both sides. The person who left decides whether contact is possible, under what conditions, and at what pace, and does not owe anyone access to their body, their home, their children, their holidays, or their private life because someone else is hurting. The person who was left decides whether they can take part in a process that may be slow, uneven, and humbling. They do not have to accept the role of permanent villain in someone else's healing story or confess to things they do not believe happened. They may have to get curious about why the other person needed that story to survive. That is hard work, and it has nothing to do with winning.

Families often confuse repair with agreement, as if healing means finally settling what really happened. Many estrangements stall right there, because the people involved cannot agree on the facts, on what the facts meant, or on how much they weighed. One person remembers a normal childhood with some hard moments. The other remembers chronic loneliness in a house that looked fine from the outside.

A relationship may not need perfect agreement to become less dangerous. It may need humility and pacing, a third party in the room, written contact before spoken contact, or an agreement that some topics are not safe yet. It may need grief for the family that never existed before anyone can build the relationship that might.

And sometimes, even with all of that, repair does not happen. Some people do not have the capacity, willingness, stability, or safety to re-enter contact. Some apologies come too late. Some boundaries stay necessary, and some family systems punish whoever tells the truth, so distance remains the only way to keep that truth alive.

Something can still change. The person who left can build a life organized around more than leaving. The person who was left can grieve without turning the grief into pursuit. Both can stop rehearsing the same argument in their heads and start telling a more honest story, one the wound no longer runs.

That may not be reconciliation. It may still be repair.

A few things to sit with

These are for sitting with, not for solving. There are no right answers.

When you imagine repair, are you imagining reunion, understanding, accountability, peace, access, or relief?

What would need to be different for contact to be emotionally safe, not just socially acceptable?

Is there an apology that would matter because it is specific, not because it is perfect?

If reconciliation never happens, what kind of internal repair is still possible?

entry.title: The Distance Between Us: Part Three
entry.summary:
Part Three: The Silence After Being Left

When someone you love stops speaking to you, grief and anger are usually there, but what tends to hit first is disorientation. For the person who was left, estrangement can feel like being sentenced without being told the charge.

More
entry.content:
Part Three: The Silence After Being Left

When someone you love stops speaking to you, grief and anger are usually there, but what tends to hit first is disorientation.

One day there is a relationship, even a strained one. Texts, holidays, obligations, the old roles and the familiar arguments, a shared history that may not be warm but is still running. Then the relationship becomes an absence. Sometimes that happens overnight. Sometimes it happens slowly enough that you only notice once it is already gone: no answer, no invitation, no explanation complete enough to hold, and no clear way back in.

For the person who was left, estrangement can feel like being sentenced without being told the charge. That does not mean there was no charge. It means the person living inside the silence may genuinely not understand what happened, or may understand pieces of it without seeing the whole shape. The mind builds a story anyway, because the nervous system does not tolerate blank space for long. So people replay the last conversation, the last holiday, the last text, the thing they said and the thing they did not say, looking for the moment they missed.

Ambiguous loss is a useful frame here. The person is alive and unreachable. The relationship is over without being dead in any ordinary way, so there is no funeral, no casserole, no socially sanctioned period of mourning. Friends do not always know what to say, and sometimes what they say makes it worse. They'll come around. You're better off. There are two sides to every story. All of it may be partly true and still miss the wound entirely. You are grieving someone who still exists, and almost nobody around you knows how to treat that as grief.

For parents this can be especially destabilizing, because the role was built around permanence. You can divorce a spouse and end a friendship, but very few people imagine parenthood as something that can be revoked. When an adult child cuts contact, the parent loses access to a person they love and often loses an organizing identity along with it: the mother, the father, the safe place, the one who tried, the one who sacrificed, the one who believed that love, even with mistakes, would count for something.

Love does count for something. It does not count for everything, and that is the sentence many people on this side of estrangement struggle to survive.

Love can be real and harm can be real in the same house. A parent may have worked, provided, stayed, worried, prayed, driven to appointments, paid tuition, and kept the household running, and still not have been experienced by their child as emotionally safe. One truth does not cancel the other, which is exactly what makes this so hard to sit inside.

Most people do not experience themselves as harmful. They experience their intentions. They remember what they meant and what they were carrying: the pressure, the childhood they came out of, the marriage they were trying to survive, the money that was never enough, the depression nobody named and the trauma nobody treated. They remember trying. Children do not live inside a parent's intentions, though. They live inside the impact.

None of that makes the parent a villain or the adult child cruel. It usually means the family contains two autobiographies that do not easily recognize each other. One says I did the best I could. The other says I know, and I was still hurt. Both can be true.

Being left tends to activate defense, and that is a nervous system response before it is a moral one. Shame is one of the most unbearable states a person can be in, and estrangement brings it very close to the surface. When shame rises, people move fast into anger, explanation, collapse, or attack. After everything I did for them. Their therapist put this in their head. They are rewriting history. They only remember the bad.

Sometimes there is a piece of truth in those thoughts. Families are complicated, and people are influenced by partners, therapists, siblings, culture, and the stories they need in order to survive. Memory is meaning-making. Even when the story feels unfair, though, the more useful question sits underneath the protest: what pain was this person trying to get away from?

Asking that is not a confession. It is not agreeing with every accusation or accepting a distorted version of yourself. It is the start of curiosity, and curiosity is usually the first thing defense destroys.

If you are the one who was left, the work is not to grovel, perform, or chase. Chasing tends to confirm, in the other person's body, that distance is necessary. The work is also not to live permanently in self-blame, because shame does not repair relationships either. It just folds people in on themselves. What is harder, and steadier, is becoming someone who can hear the impact without immediately defending the intention. Someone who can say there are parts I remember differently, and I still want to understand what it was like for you, who can tolerate not being seen as only good, who can grieve without turning the grief into pressure.

The person who left may be watching for one thing more than anything else. Not whether you are sad, or whether you miss them, or whether you can explain yourself, but whether being in contact with you still requires them to abandon themselves.

A few things to sit with

These are for sitting with, not for solving. There are no right answers.

When you think about the estrangement, what emotion arrives first: grief, anger, shame, fear, confusion, or something else?

What story do you tell yourself about why this happened? Which parts of that story are known, and which parts are guesses?

Can you name the difference between what you intended and what the other person may have experienced?

If this person never fully agrees with your version of the story, what kind of repair would still be meaningful?

What Family Estrangement Distance Solves, and What It Does Not

I am going to say the thing family estrangement advice usually dances around. Cutting off contact often works. That is exactly why people do it. It is not a failed strategy. It is a strategy that delivers, at least at first.

When you leave a defensive relationship, real things change. The dread lifts. Sleep returns. You stop rehearsing conversations in the shower. People often describe this relief. They gain room to breathe. They find space to become themselves. Let me be clear. If distance restored your life, that is significant. No one gets to talk you out of it.

Here is the harder part. Ending the harm is not the same as healing from it. Relief is real, and relief matters. But relief is not repair. Whatever hurt you is still there underneath, whether or not you are looking at it. Distance buys you the conditions to do the deeper work. It does not do the work for you.

So let me separate the two.

Here is what distance reliably solves. It stops the ongoing harm. It interrupts a pattern that was wearing you down. It gives the protective part of you the win it has been fighting for. Those are real victories. They matter.

Here is what distance usually does not solve. It rarely gives you the thing the wounded part actually wanted. And that thing was almost never silence. The younger part wanted to be seen. Believed. Treated as if its experience was real. Cutting contact ends the harm, but it does not hand you that. So the longing does not disappear. It goes underground. It shows up at the wedding you skip. In the half-second of panic when a stranger has your mother's laugh. In the dream where everyone is at the table and you are not.

Researchers call this ambiguous loss. The person is still out there, alive, reachable in theory, and gone in fact. There is no funeral, no ending, no closure, because nothing has actually concluded. And that ambiguity does not only haunt the person who was left. It follows the one who left, too.

Leaving the protector in charge has a cost. It is easy to miss this cost. It does not announce itself. A part on guard for years may not stand down. This happens even after the threat is gone. It keeps scanning. Sometimes, the vigilance spreads. It shows up in other relationships. This happens with a partner. You watch for signs of them becoming like a parent. Friendships are held slightly at arm's length. There's a quiet certainty. Closeness will eventually be used against you.

The estrangement stopped one source of harm. But the required guard can quietly tax everything else. This is not a reason to reopen a closed door. Ensure the protector isn't running the house. Its job was to guard one room.

Once the bleeding stops, the question changes. It is no longer about justified estrangement. It almost certainly was justified. The new question is quieter. Is your protector responding to a current threat? Or is it defending against a past one? Nervous systems update slowly. A part learned danger at fifteen. It will run that program at forty. This happens even if facts have shifted. That is not weakness. That is how survival wiring works.

Let me draw a careful line, because this is where a few people misread me. Some estrangements should stay exactly as they are. When the threat is current, when contact means abuse, manipulation, or the steady erosion of your sense of reality, distance is not avoidance. It is good clinical sense, and sometimes it is survival. I am not nudging anyone toward a reunion their body is still saying no to.

What I am asking is narrower. Is your distance something you keep choosing, with your eyes open? Or is it a program still running on its own from a decision you made in crisis years ago? Both can be valid. Only one of them is a choice.

Distance cannot do the deepest work for you. Thank your protector self. It helped you escape. The younger part it guarded needs tending. You must tend to it. This applies whether the other person changes. It applies whether they apologize. It applies if they stay alive. That work moves the loss through you. The cutoff gave you safety to begin. It was never going to finish it.

A few things to sit with

Setting the relationship aside for a moment, what does the younger, hurt part of you still long for? Has the silence given it that, or only protected it?

Honestly check your defense. Are you defending against who they are now? Or who they were when the wound was made? How would you know the difference?

Is your distance a conscious re-choice? Or is it running on its own? Have you not looked at it in a while?

What would it mean to tend the wound yourself, without waiting for the other person to make it right?

entry.title: The Distance Between Us: Part One
entry.summary:
The Distance Between Us

Estrangement is one of the most common losses almost no one talks about. More than a quarter of adults have cut off contact with a family member at some point. That is tens of millions of people, and most of them say it still weighs on them. So if you are carrying this, you are not the exception. You are part of a very large, very quiet group that mostly suffers in private.

This series looks at estrangement from both ends of the silence. The first two essays sit with the person who needed distance. The last two sit with the person who was left. I am not here to talk anyone into reconciling, and I am not here to talk anyone out of protecting themselves. I am here because both sides usually get flattened into a cartoon. The cold, ungrateful child. The toxic, unrepentant parent. Almost no one is actually living inside the cartoon. They are living inside a nervous system that did the best it could with what it had.

One note on language. When I say the person who needed distance and the person who was left, I am using rough shorthand. Estrangement happens between siblings, between partners and in-laws, between friends who were family in everything but name. Use whatever fits your situation.

entry.content:
A Four-Part Series on Family Estrangement, From Both Sides


Family estrangement is one of the most common losses almost no one talks about. More than a quarter of adults have cut off contact with a family member at some point. That is tens of millions of people, and most of them say it still weighs on them. So if you are carrying this, you are not the exception. You are part of a very large, very quiet group that mostly suffers in private.

This series looks at estrangement from both ends of the silence. The first two essays sit with the person who needed distance. The last two sit with the person who was left. I don't talk anyone into reconciling. I don't talk anyone out of protecting themselves. Both sides usually get flattened into a cartoon. The cold, ungrateful child. The toxic, unrepentant parent. Almost no one is actually living inside this cartoon. They live inside a nervous system. It did the best it could with what it had.

One note on language. When I say the person who needed distance and the person who was left, I am using rough shorthand. Estrangement happens between siblings, between partners and in-laws, between friends who were family in everything but name. Use whatever fits your situation.


Part One: The Logic of Leaving Family 

People assume that cutting off family is cruelty. From the outside it can look like punishment. From the inside it almost never feels that way. It feels like the last door left.

Here is what most people miss. We are built to stay. From birth, we seek closeness to those who raised us. That wiring does not switch off. It stays even when those people hurt us. A child reaches for a frightening parent. Connection is older and stronger than judging danger. We are designed to move toward family, not away.

So when someone finally cuts contact, they are not taking the easy road. They are overriding one of the deepest instincts they have. That takes enormous force. And that force does not come from one bad holiday. It comes from years.

Most of the time, the body decides first. If you have ever felt your stomach drop when a certain name lit up your phone, you already know this. The shoulders climb. The breath goes shallow. Sleep gets worse for a week before every visit. The nervous system has been filing reports for a long time. The decision to leave is often the mind finally agreeing with what the body has been saying all along.

This is what we mean by "the body keeps the score". Hard relationships are not stored as tidy, recited memories. They get stored as states. The clench. The brace. A sense that something is wrong appears before any explanation. Many who cut contact cannot point to one dramatic justifying event. Instead, they have a body that learned this cost too much. Across a thousand small moments, the relationship cost more than it could pay. The absence of a single wound does not mean no injury. It usually means the injury was steady.

Polyvagal theory gives us a simple map. When a relationship reads as a threat, the system gets stuck in defense. Some people live keyed up around a family member. They are vigilant, braced for the next thing. Others go flat and checked out, just waiting for it to be over. Neither is a place where a person can live well. And here is what almost no one says out loud. For some, the first full breath in years comes after they stop answering the phone. Distance is not avoidance. It lets the body settle long enough to think.

There is a cruel irony here, and it causes a lot of misunderstanding. The person who leaves often looks calm. They go quiet. They get organized. They seem almost cold about it. And everyone around them reads that composure as proof that they never cared.

It is the opposite. When staying close is too painful, the system learns to turn the longing down. To act as if the need is not there, because feeling the full force of it would be unbearable. The flatness is not the absence of love. It is love with the volume forced down so the person can function. Some of the most detached-looking people I have sat with were working hardest to keep a flood from breaking through.

Parts work names this clearly. We are not single, unified selves. We are made of parts, many of them shaped by survival. The part that cuts contact is almost always a protector. Its whole job is to stand guard over a younger, more wounded part. The one who was dismissed, frightened, or made responsible for an adult's feelings long before that was fair. The protector watched that younger part get hurt enough times and finally said, never again.

From that angle, estrangement is not a personal failure. It is a protector doing exactly what it was built to do. Survive.

I want to be honest about one thing, because false comfort helps no one. Naming the cutoff as protective does not make it free, and it does not make it final. A protector can keep you safe and still keep you stuck. We will get to that next. For now, this is enough. If you needed distance, you were almost certainly responding to something real. The body does not mount that kind of defense over nothing. The healing begins when we start to listen to and trust our deepest knowing. Our self. 


A few things to sit with

These are for sitting with, not for solving. There are no right answers.

1. When you imagine contact with this person, what happens in your body first, before any thought arrives? Where do you feel it?

2. If the part of you that wanted distance could speak, what is it trying to protect? How old does that protected part feel?

3. Was the distance something you chose, or something your body chose and your mind agreed to later?

4. What did you gain in the quiet that you could not reach when you were still in contact?

If you feel compelled to start a conversation, comment or DM. As always I am very curious about what you think.
